title: With Taalas, AMD Can Bake AI Inference Directly Into Its Chippery
gist: Nvidia's own GTC 2026 data showed GPUs cannot economically drive more than ~400 tokens per second per user, so inference must be disaggregated — prefill on GPUs, decode on SRAM-heavy deterministic engines — which explains Nvidia's $20 billion Grok acquihire. AMD faces the identical GPU decode limitation and, unable to afford a $50.9 billion Cerebras, is partnering with Cerebras near-term while acquiring Taalas, whose HC chips hard-code model weights into ROM linked to on-chip SRAM KV cache, ushering in Model Specific Architectures.

themes.theme: GPU decode ceiling exposed by Nvidia

insights.claim: Jensen Huang disclosed at GTC 2026 in March that customers needing low-latency inference for agentic AI or premium chattybot service cannot achieve it on GPU architectures alone.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The GPU vendor itself conceding a hard ceiling on its own architecture legitimizes the entire non-GPU inference accelerator category.
insights.locator: Jensen Huang, the chief executive officer

insights.claim: The prescribed fix is to split inference so prefill (processing context-window input tokens) runs on GPU clusters while decode (generating responses) is offloaded to massively parallel, deterministic, SRAM-heavy matrix engines.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Disaggregated inference is the architectural template every hyperscaler will copy — it splits the accelerator TAM into two distinct, separately-sourced markets.
insights.locator: What Huang showed was that to get the best

insights.claim: GPUs are excellent high-bandwidth general-purpose parallel engines but their performance on the decode phase of inference is less deterministic than ideal, which is the root cause of the interactivity ceiling.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Determinism, not raw FLOPS, is the spec that matters for high-interactivity inference — a criterion that favors fixed-function silicon over GPUs.
insights.locator: The reason is simple enough

insights.claim: GPU accelerators alone cannot drive more than 400 tokens per second per user at reasonable overall system throughput.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: 400 TPS/user is the hard boundary that defines where non-GPU decode silicon becomes mandatory rather than optional.
insights.quote: You can plainly see that GPU accelerators alone really can’t drive more than 400 TPS/user at a reasonable overall system throughput.
insights.locator: The whole new Ultra tier of inference

insights.claim: A Grace CG100 CPU plus Hopper H100 GPU node handles roughly 100 tokens per second per user by batching users and then peters out, defining Huang's medium performance tier.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline against which every subsequent Nvidia generation is marketed — useful for sanity-checking vendor uplift claims.
insights.locator: Huang’s charts at GTC showed

insights.claim: The NVL72 platform with 18 Grace CPUs and 36 Blackwell B300 GPUs delivers about 3.5X the tokens per second per megawatt of the Grace-Hopper system at the 100 TPS interactivity level.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: TPS per megawatt is the real efficiency currency for inference buyers, since power, not silicon, is the constrained input.
insights.locator: The NVL72 hybrid CPU-GPU platforms

insights.claim: An NVL72 rackscale system using Vera CV100 CPUs and Rubin R200 GPUs delivers roughly 2X the TPS/MW of the Grace-Blackwell system and 7X that of the Grace-Hopper system.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A 7X efficiency gain over two generations sets the depreciation clock for anyone still buying Hopper-class inference capacity.
insights.locator: An impending NVL72 rackscale system

insights.claim: At the Premium tier of 400 TPS/user interactivity, Grace-Blackwell rackscale TPS/MW falls very close to zero while Vera-Rubin delivers roughly 10X better and still reasonable throughput.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Efficiency collapsing to near zero at high interactivity means current-generation fleets simply cannot serve premium agentic products at any sane cost.
insights.locator: Out at a Premium tier, with 400 TPS interactivity

insights.claim: Putting decode on a rack of Grok LP30 accelerators opens an entirely new Ultra tier of inference with upwards of 1,000 TPS/user, the presumed baseline for agentic workloads.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: If agentic AI needs ~1,000 TPS/user, a whole performance tier exists that GPUs cannot reach at all — a structural demand pull for dedicated decode silicon.
insights.locator: The whole new Ultra tier of inference

insights.claim: At the Premium tier, a Vera-Rubin NVL72 paired with Grok accelerators reaches 35X the performance of a Grace-Blackwell NVL72, versus only 10X for Vera-Rubin without Grok.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Most of the headline generational gain at high interactivity comes from the non-GPU decode engine, not the new GPU — a critical attribution for infrastructure buyers.
insights.locator: Not only that, the Premium tier

insights.claim: There are unknown scaling limits on how far a Grok decode cluster can be extended, since you cannot link a million such devices together to push interactivity higher.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Undisclosed scaling ceilings on decode accelerators are the unpriced risk in the disaggregated inference thesis.
insights.locator: Of course, there are limited to how far

insights.claim: The GPU decode ceiling explains both Nvidia's $20 billion acquihire of the Grok team and technology in December and AMD's parallel moves toward non-GPU inference silicon.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Ties a $20B transaction directly to a measurable architectural limit — a template for predicting the next accelerator acquisitions.
insights.locator: This pair of charts not only explain

insights.claim: AMD acquired AI inference startup Taalas for an undisclosed sum as a genuine acquisition rather than a scrutiny-avoiding acquihire, because AMD's GPUs share the same inference-decode limitations as Nvidia's.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Structuring it as a real acquisition rather than an acquihire signals AMD intends to own and productize the IP, not just absorb engineers.
insights.quote: not some dubious, scrutiny-avoiding acquihire, but a real acquisition
insights.locator: but it also explains why AMD is partnering with Cerebras

insights.claim: AMD cannot control Cerebras technology because Cerebras raised heavily and went public earlier this year, reaching a $50.9 billion market capitalization that could require roughly $60 billion to acquire.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Cerebras' IPO effectively priced itself out of an AMD takeout, forcing partnership instead of ownership — a structural constraint on AMD's stack strategy.
insights.locator: The only trouble is, AMD does not control Cerebras technology

insights.claim: Cerebras is making just under $200 million in revenue per quarter, implying an acquisition would cost roughly 300X annual revenue against a market norm of about one-tenth that premium.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: An explicit 300X-versus-30X valuation gap is a concrete bear marker on Cerebras' post-IPO price and on any acquisition speculation.
insights.quote: Paying 300X annual revenue is very risky in a world that pays maybe one-tenth of that premium.
insights.locator: AMD increasingly likes to control its own stack

insights.claim: Cerebras was AMD's only available partner because Graphcore was absorbed by Softbank (owner of Arm), Nvidia essentially bought Grok, and SambaNova partnered with Intel.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The independent inference-accelerator field has been fully paired off — remaining startups become scarce, strategically valuable assets.
insights.locator: Hence, it looks like AMD will partner for now

insights.claim: The AMD-Cerebras partnership is expected to pair a fourth-generation waferscale engine (WSE-4), due to be announced later this year, with AMD Helios clusters using Verano Epyc CPUs and Altair MI455X GPUs for disaggregated inference.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term product pairing to watch — it is AMD's direct answer to Nvidia's Vera-Rubin plus LPU combination.
insights.locator: The Cerebras partnership is a good thing

insights.claim: Taalas was founded by engineers from RISC-V and AI accelerator company Tenstorrent, and hard-codes AI inference models and their weights into ROM circuits linked to giant SRAM blocks acting as an on-chip KV cache.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Baking weights into metal eliminates memory-bandwidth as the inference bottleneck entirely — the most radical departure from the HBM-centric accelerator model.
insights.locator: I did a deep dive on Taalas back in February

insights.claim: Taalas' current HC1 chip generation can store an 8-billion-parameter model and the next-generation HC2 was slated for 20 billion parameters, with a few tens of interlinked chips theoretically holding trillion-parameter models.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Per-chip parameter capacity is the gating spec for whether this approach can serve frontier models rather than only small ones.
insights.locator: The current HC1 generation of Taalas chips

insights.claim: In initial benchmarks Taalas shows extremely low latencies and much lower cost per token for inference than Nvidia Blackwell B200 GPUs.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Cost per token versus B200 is the metric that determines whether AMD can undercut Nvidia on inference economics rather than compete on training.
insights.locator: In initial benchmark tests, Taalas is showing

insights.claim: Each model requires its own HC1 chiplet variant, changing only the two metal layers that encode the model and weights while the SRAM and surrounding components stay identical.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Limiting customization to two metal layers keeps mask costs and turnaround low enough to make per-model silicon commercially plausible.
insights.locator: The trick with Taalas is that each model

insights.claim: Taalas claims it costs 100X as much money to train a new GenAI model as it does to customize an HC chip and buy it in reasonable volumes, plausibly a few hundred thousand units.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: If custom silicon costs 1 percent of a training run, every serious model owner has an economic case to tape out its own inference chip.
insights.locator: But, then again, Taalas says it takes 100X

insights.claim: AMD has said only that it plans to integrate Taalas technology into its accelerator roadmap and develop system-level solutions with AMD Instinct GPUs, marking the arrival of Model Specific Architectures.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Model Specific Architectures would fragment inference silicon by model rather than by vendor — a new axis of lock-in and a new obsolescence risk.
insights.quote: AMD plans to integrate the technology into its accelerator roadmap and develop system-level solutions with AMD Instinct GPUs.
insights.locator: AMD is not saying much about its plans for Taalas
